comparability.reason: This record focuses on CaO-amended smoldering tests where CaF2 formation was characterized, allowing conditional comparison of defluorination and product speciation against no-CaO tests and aggregate fluorine mass balance results within the same soil-smoldering system.

endpoints.interpretation: XPS showed CaF2 was absent in CaO and pretreatment soils but present in post-treatment soils, and authors inferred that >98% of the pretreatment PFAS mass was converted to CaF2. This supports extensive defluorination and conversion of organofluorine to inorganic fluoride solid, but carbon mineralization was not directly assessed.
endpoints.reported_term: >98% of pretreatment PFAS mass mineralized into CaF2

endpoints.interpretation: Authors interpret the strong CaF2 signal and low HF emissions as evidence that PFAS were mineralized to CaF2 during smoldering with CaO, minimizing potentially harmful emissions. The measured endpoint is fluorine partitioning and speciation (CaF2 vs HF vs organic fluorine), not direct CO2 production.
endpoints.reported_term: PFAS mineralized with minimal HF emissions

limitations.statement: CaF2 formation was inferred from XPS signals, which are qualitative/semi-quantitative and do not provide a full fluorine mass balance for CaF2 alone; thus, the >98% estimate of PFAS mass converted to CaF2 carries analytical uncertainty.

records.citation: Wood RJ, Sidnell T, Ross I, et al. Ultrasonic degradation of perfluorooctane sulfonic acid (PFOS) correlated with sonochemical and sonoluminescence characterisation. Ultrason Sonochem. 2020;68:105196.

comparability.reason: The study provides qualitative and semi-quantitative evidence of PFOS parent loss, stoichiometric inorganic fluoride release, and low yields of targeted short-chain PFAAs under specific ultrasonic frequencies and time scales. However, key conditions such as exact initial PFOS concentration, reactor configuration, and full fluorine mass balance (including non-target organofluorine species and mineralization products like CO2) are not fully specified in the supplied text, limiting direct quantitative comparison with other PFAS destruction technologies on a common basis.

endpoints.interpretation: Loss of PFOS parent compound in solution during sonication, measured analytically (ALS). Authors describe "degradation" and report complete PFOS degradation at 400 and 500 kHz after several hours.
endpoints.reported_term: PFOS degradation; complete degradation at selected frequencies

endpoints.interpretation: Inorganic fluoride release to solution, compared with the theoretical fluoride yield (315.9 µM, 6.001 mg L-1) corresponding to complete cleavage of C–F bonds from PFOS. Authors report stoichiometric release of fluoride ions at 400, 500, and 1000 kHz, supporting extensive defluorination under these conditions.
endpoints.reported_term: Stoichiometric fluoride release; 100% PFOS degradation theoretical fluoride yield

endpoints.interpretation: Formation of shorter-chain PFAAs as measurable transformation products; total mass of these species is less than 1% of the total yield by mass, indicating limited accumulation of identifiable perfluoroalkyl acid intermediates.
endpoints.reported_term: Trace shorter chain PFAAs as transformation products

endpoints.interpretation: Time-dependent fluoride release evaluated and compared to zero-order kinetics at different frequencies; within the first 2 h, 400 kHz shows least and 1000 kHz the best agreement with zero-order behaviour, but this is a kinetic characterization rather than a separate degradation endpoint.
endpoints.reported_term: Kinetic behaviour (zero-order agreement) in fluoride release

limitations.statement: Single-compound PFOS system in a simple aqueous matrix; results may not extrapolate to mixed PFAS or real wastewaters.

Fluorine mass balance is based on inorganic fluoride and targeted short-chain PFAAs; other inorganic or organic fluorine-containing products (e.g., volatile organofluorine or unidentified organics) are not comprehensively quantified, so complete destruction versus defluorination cannot be fully resolved.
Bench-scale ultrasonic reactor and controlled conditions may not represent performance at larger scales or under variable field conditions.

matrix.value: Simple aqueous PFOS solution (laboratory water matrix, not a complex wastewater).

operating_conditions.name: Ultrasonic frequency
operating_conditions.qualifiers: 44 kHz reported as ineffective for PFOS degradation; stoichiometric fluoride release and complete PFOS degradation reported at 400 and 500 kHz; stoichiometric fluoride release reported at 1000 kHz.

operating_conditions.qualifiers: Degradation of PFOS and fluoride release after 4 h of sonication reported; kinetics within first 2 h also discussed.

residuals_byproducts.statement: Trace concentrations of several shorter-chain PFAAs were detected at all ultrasonic frequencies; collectively they accounted for less than 1% of the total yield by mass, indicating only minor accumulation of these identifiable transformation products.

Authors state that stoichiometric fluoride release and complete PFOS degradation at 400 and 500 kHz occurred "without significant formation of less fluorinated shorter chain PFAAs," implying that most fluorine was converted to inorganic fluoride rather than remaining in measurable PFAAs; other organofluorine products, if present, were not fully characterized in the supplied text.

treatment.value: Ultrasonic (sonolytic) treatment of PFOS solution at various ultrasonic frequencies, with characterization of sonochemical and sonoluminescence conditions.

records.citation: Li J, Austin C, Moore S, Pinkard BR, Novosselov IV. PFOS destruction in a continuous supercritical water oxidation reactor. Chem Eng J. 2023;451:139063.

comparability.reason: Bench-scale continuous SCWO experiments on a defined aqueous PFAS matrix with clearly specified temperature and residence-time conditions, fluorine mass balance, and parent PFAS measurements provide quantitatively interpretable removal, defluorination, and reported mineralization endpoints that can be compared to other destructive treatments under similarly controlled conditions and concentration-based metrics.

endpoints.interpretation: Loss of PFOS, PFHpS, and PFOA parent compounds in the aqueous phase; authors describe up to 99.999% destruction at 650 °C and ~30 s, but this endpoint reflects parent-PFAS concentration decrease rather than, by itself, chemical destruction.
endpoints.reported_term: destruction

endpoints.interpretation: Defluorination assessed by measuring aqueous fluoride concentration and constructing a fluorine mass balance relative to initial PFAS fluorine; complete defluorination reported at 650 °C and ~30 s, with F-balance exceeding 100% at T > 580 °C and deficits at lower temperatures.
endpoints.reported_term: complete defluorination; fluorine mass balance

endpoints.interpretation: Authors report 99.9999% mineralization at T > 650 °C, interpreted as nearly complete conversion of PFAS fluorine to inorganic fluoride combined with disappearance of organic PFAS. The provided text does not describe a full carbon balance, so the mineralization percentage appears to be inferred primarily from PFAS loss and fluorine mass balance rather than a direct CO2-based carbon-fate measurement.
endpoints.reported_term: 99.9999% mineralization of PFAS

endpoints.interpretation: Total fluorine balance constructed from measured PFAS and fluoride concentrations; >100% F recovery at T > 580 °C and deficits at lower T indicate temperature-dependent closure of the fluorine balance and possible contributions from unquantified fluorinated species or measurement uncertainty.
endpoints.reported_term: overall fluorine mass balance

limitations.statement: Evidence for mineralization is primarily based on fluorine mass balance and PFAS disappearance, with only qualitative mention of gas-phase CO2; a complete carbon balance is not documented in the provided text.

Reported defluorination and mineralization efficiencies are obtained at relatively high temperatures (>=580-650 °C) and short residence time (~30 s) in a specialized SCWO reactor, which may limit direct transferability to other treatment systems or lower-temperature processes.

comparability.reason: Gas-phase VOF occurrence and persistence are characterized semi-qualitatively without concentration or flux data or detection limits, providing valuable mechanistic insight into transformation pathways and potential unidentified fluorine compartments, but not directly comparable in a quantitative sense to other treatments focused on aqueous-phase removal or defluorination percentages.

endpoints.interpretation: Gas-phase GC/MS analysis shows formation of volatile organofluorines at lower SCWO temperatures, indicating transformation of aqueous PFAS into intermediate volatile fluorinated species rather than direct defluorination; these VOFs persist longer than PFCAs in the effluent.
endpoints.reported_term: volatile organofluorines (VOFs) as intermediates

endpoints.interpretation: At 580 °C, no gaseous fluorine-containing compounds were detected and only N2, O2, CO2, and H2O were present, implying that above this temperature most fluorine is present as inorganic fluoride in the aqueous phase rather than as volatile organofluorines, consistent with high defluorination and reduced off-gas PFAS-related emissions.
endpoints.reported_term: absence of gaseous fluorine compounds at 580 °C

endpoints.interpretation: Authors note that VOFs were more persistent than PFCA in effluent, suggesting that these gas-phase or semi-volatile organofluorine transformation products can control the residence time needed to achieve high overall defluorination, even when parent PFAS appear largely degraded.
endpoints.reported_term: VOFs more persistent than PFCA in effluent

limitations.statement: Gas-phase analysis of volatile organofluorines was semi-qualitative by GC/MS, and the specific compounds and their concentrations were not fully quantified in the provided text, limiting the ability to close a complete fluorine and carbon mass balance across all phases.

Lack of reported detection limits for gaseous fluorinated species means that non-detection at 580 °C cannot be directly translated into a quantitative upper bound on residual volatile organofluorines.

residuals_byproducts.statement: At lower SCWO temperatures, gas-phase GC/MS detected ion fragments associated with volatile organofluorines, indicating formation of fluorinated intermediates in the gas phase during PFOS and PFOA destruction.
VOFs were found to be more persistent than PFCA in the effluent, and their stability may dictate the minimum residence time required to achieve high defluorination efficiencies in SCWO.
